Boundedness to a logistic chemotaxis system
with singular sensitivity

Xiangdong Zhao ††thanks: E-mail: zhaoxd1223@163.com (X. D. Zhao) Affiliation: School of Mathematics, Liaoning Normal University, Dalian 116029, P.R. China
Abstract

In this paper, we study the parabolic-elliptic Keller-Segel system with singular sensitivity and logistic-type source: ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(uv∇v)+ru−μuku_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(\frac{u}{v}\nabla v)+ru-\mu u^{k}, 0=Δ​v−v+u0=\Delta v-v+u under the non-flux boundary conditions in a smooth bounded convex domain Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, χ,r,μ>0\chi,r,\mu>0, k>1k>1 and n≥2n\geq 2. It is shown that the system possesses a globally bounded classical solution if k>3​n−2nk>\frac{3n-2}{n}, and r>χ24r>\frac{\chi^{2}}{4} for 0<χ≤20<\chi\leq 2, or r>χ−1r>\chi-1 for χ>2\chi>2. In addition, under the same condition for r,χr,\chi, the system admits a global generalized solution when k∈(2−1n,3​n−2n]k\in(2-\frac{1}{n},\frac{3n-2}{n}], moreover this global generalized solution should be globally bounded provided rμ\frac{r}{\mu} and the initial data u0u_{0} suitably small.

35K55; 35B45; 35B40; 92C17

Keywords:

Keller-Segel system; Singular sensitivity; Logistic source; Boundedness

1 Introduction

Chemotaxis, is a spontaneous cross-diffusion phenomena by which organisms direct their movements in regard to a stimulating chemical. In 1970, Keller and Segel proposed a model to represent the chemotaxis phenomena, i.e., the oriented or partially oriented movement of cells with respect to a chemical signal produced by the cells themselves [1]:

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(uv∇v),x∈Ω,t>0,τ​vt=Δ​v−v+u,x∈Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(\frac{u}{v}\nabla v),&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\[4.0pt] \displaystyle\tau v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\end{array}\right.

where τ∈{0,1}\tau\in\{0,1\},χ>0\chi>0. The singular chemotactic sensitive function χv\frac{\chi}{v} with χ>0\chi>0 is derived by the Weber-Fechner law on the response of the cells uu to the stimulating chemical signal vv. With the singularity determined by the sensitive function χv\frac{\chi}{v}, the cellular movements are governed by the taxis flux χ∇vv\frac{\chi\nabla v}{v}, which may be unbounded when v≈0v\approx 0. Different to the classical Keller-Segel model (i.e., replacing the singular sensitive function χv\frac{\chi}{v} by the constant function χ\chi in (1)), it is important to obtain a lower bound on vv for studying the global dynamical behavior. This can be achieved by a pointwise estimate [2]

v⁡(x,t)≥c0​∫Ωu⁡(x,t)​𝑑x,x∈Ω,t>0\displaystyle v(x,t)\geq c_{0}\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)dx,~~~~~~~x\in\Omega,~t>0

with c0=c0​(|Ω|,n)>0c_{0}=c_{0}(|\Omega|,n)>0. Due to the mass conservation of cells uu in system (1), it is known that the singularity involved in sensitive function χv\frac{\chi}{v} is in fact absent. Generally, chemotactic sensitive coefficient χ>0\chi>0 properly small benefits the global existence-boundedness of solutions to system (1), which can be presented in [3, 6, 5, 8, 7, 4]. It is pointed that for the parabolic-elliptic case of the system (1) (τ=0)(\tau=0) with radial assumption, Nagai and Senba proved that the problem admits a finite time blow-up solution [9] if χ>2​nn−2\chi>\frac{2n}{n-2} with n≥3n\geq 3, and ∫Ωu0​|x|2​𝑑x\int_{\Omega}u_{0}|x|^{2}dx sufficiently small.

Consider the chemotaxis system as follows

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+ru−μuk,x∈Ω,t>0,τ​vt=Δ​v−v+u,x∈Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+ru-\mu u^{k},&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\[4.0pt] \displaystyle\tau v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\[4.0pt] \end{array}\right.

where χ,r,μ>0\chi,r,\mu>0, k>1k>1 and τ∈{0,1}\tau\in\{0,1\}. Such self-limiting growth mechanism involved in the logistic-type source generally benefits the global dynamic of solutions. For parabolic-elliptic case of (1) (τ=0\tau=0 ), the system with k=2k=2 possesses a global weak solution if μ>0\mu>0 and a global bounded classical solution if μ>n−2n​χ\mu>\frac{n-2}{n}\chi [10]. If k>2−1nk>2-\frac{1}{n} with n≥1n\geq 1, there exists a global very weak solution, which is globally bounded provided μ\mu sufficiently large and u0u_{0} sufficiently small [11]. Replacing 0=Δ​v−v+u0=\Delta v-v+u in (1) by 0=Δ​v−m⁡(t)+u0=\Delta v-m(t)+u with m⁡(t):=1|Ω|​∫Ωu⁡(x,t)​𝑑xm(t):=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)dx, it is shown with radial assumption that the system admits a finite time blow-up solution if 1<k<32+12​n−21<k<\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2n-2} with n≥5n\geq 5 [12]. For the parabolic-parabolic case of (1) (τ=1\tau=1), if k=2k=2, n=2n=2 [13], or n≥3n\geq 3 with μ>0\mu>0 sufficiently large [14], the problem possesses globally bounded classical solutions. If k>2−1nk>2-\frac{1}{n} with n≥1n\geq 1, there exists global very weak solutions [15], which are globally bounded provided rμ\frac{r}{\mu} and the initial data all sufficiently small for n=3n=3 [16]. In addition, more properties of solutions to (1) can be found in [17, 18, 19].

Recall the chemotaxis system with singular sensitivity and logistic source

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(uv∇v)+ru−μuk,x∈Ω,t>0,τ​vt=Δ​v−v+u,x∈Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(\frac{u}{v}\nabla v)+ru-\mu u^{k},&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\[4.0pt] \displaystyle\tau v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\end{array}\right.

where χ,r,μ>0\chi,r,\mu>0, k>1k>1 and τ∈{0,1}\tau\in\{0,1\}. The difficulty in studying global solvability of solutions comes from the hazardous combination of singular sensitive chemotactic mechanism and the self-limiting growth mechanism involved in logistic source. Due to missing the mass conservation for uu, the singularity contained in chemotactic term may be presence. Similarity to system (1), the suitable smallness of chemotactic sensitive coefficient χ>0\chi>0 is necessary to establish global existence-boundedness of solutions to system (1). If n,k=2n,k=2, there exists a unique globally bounded classical solution [20, 21], whenever

r>{χ24,0<χ≤2,χ−1,χ>2.r>\begin{cases}&\frac{\chi^{2}}{4},~~~~0<\chi\leq 2,\\ &\chi-1,~~~~\chi>2.\end{cases} (1.10)

In addition, the author has proved for k>2−1nk>2-\frac{1}{n} that the system (1) with τ=1\tau=1 possesses a global very weak solution provided χ\chi suitably small related to r,kr,k [22].

Turn to a chemotaxis-consumption model of the type

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(uv∇v)+ru−μuk,x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−u​v,x∈Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(\frac{u}{v}\nabla v)+ru-\mu u^{k},&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\[4.0pt] \displaystyle v_{t}=\Delta v-uv,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\[4.0pt] \end{array}\right.

where χ,r,μ>0\chi,r,\mu>0 and k>1k>1. It seems difficult to study the global existence and further global dynamic behavior of solutions to (1) than that for the problems (1) and (1). The troubles lie in the interplay of the consumptive effect with the singular chemotactic mechanism and self-limiting logistic source. Intuitively, the oxygen vv shrinks in (1)2 during evolution, and then enhances the chemotactic strength of the bacteria because of the singular behavior when v≈0v\approx 0 in (1)1. This implies the singularity in chemotactic sensitive function χv\frac{\chi}{v} should be persistence. Recall some results on the case of k=2k=2. It is shown for n≥2n\geq 2 that there exists a global classical solution if 0<χ<2n0<\chi<\sqrt{\frac{2}{n}} and μ>n−22​n\mu>\frac{n-2}{2n}, and that for n=1n=1 the global classical solution is globally bounded if χ,r,μ>0\chi,r,\mu>0 [23]. Moreover, the problem for n≥1n\geq 1 possesses a global generalized solution [24]. If k>1+n2k>1+\frac{n}{2}, the author has established the global solvability of classical solutions [25]. We refer to [26, 27, 28] for more results on chemotaxis-consumption system without logistic source.

In this paper, we consider the following parabolic-elliptic chemotaxis system with singular sensitivity and logistic-type source

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(uv∇v)+ru−μuk,x∈Ω,t>0,0=Δ​v−v+u,x∈Ω,t>0,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),x∈Ω,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(\frac{u}{v}\nabla v)+ru-\mu u^{k},&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\[4.0pt] \displaystyle 0=\Delta v-v+u,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\[4.0pt] \displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial{\nu}}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial{\nu}}=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,~t>0,\\[4.0pt] \displaystyle u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega,\end{array}\right.

where χ,r,μ>0\chi,r,\mu>0, k>1k>1. Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n≥2)(n\geq 2) is a smooth bounded convex domain, ∂∂ν\frac{\partial}{\partial\nu} denotes the derivation with respect to the outer normal of ∂Ω\partial\Omega, and the initial data

u0​(x)∈C0​(Ω¯),u0​(x)≥0​and​u0​(x)≠0,x∈Ω¯.\displaystyle u_{0}(x)\in C^{0}(\overline{\Omega}),~u_{0}(x)\geq 0{\rm~and~}u_{0}(x)\neq 0,~x\in\overline{\Omega}. (1.19)

ukanduv∇vbelongtoLloc1(Ω×(0,∞)),\displaystyle u^{k}~{\rm and}~\frac{u}{v}\nabla v~{\rm belong~to}~L_{\rm loc}^{1}(\Omega\times(0,\infty)),

and moreover

−∫0∞∫Ωuφt−∫Ωu0φ(⋅,0)≤∫0∞∫ΩuΔφ+χ∫0∞∫Ωuv∇v⋅∇φ\displaystyle-\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}u\varphi_{t}-\int_{\Omega}u_{0}\varphi(\cdot,0)\leq\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}u\Delta\varphi+\chi\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}\frac{u}{v}\nabla v\cdot\nabla\varphi

and the equality (1.21) hold for all φ\varphi and ψ\psi satisfying (1.22) and (1.23).

Definition 1.3

A couple of function (u,v)(u,v) will be called a generalized solution to (1) if it is both a very weak subsolution and a weak logarithmic supersolution of (1).

To obtain the global dynamic behavior of solution to system (1) for general k>1k>1, we will at first establish a positive uniform-in-time lower bound for chemical signal vv. With the aid of a crucial ODE inequality [29], this will be realized by a uniform-in-time upper estimate on the integral ∫Ωu−m​𝑑x\int_{\Omega}u^{-m}dx with some m>0m>0. Furthermore, via a standard process on energy estimate for ∫Ωup​𝑑x\int_{\Omega}u^{p}dx with p>1p>1, we conclude the global boundedness of the classical solutions if k>3​n−2nk>\frac{3n-2}{n} and χ>0\chi>0 suitably small relative to r>0r>0.

In order to deal with the global generalized solution of classical parabolic-elliptic system (1)(i.e., without singular sensitive function 1v\frac{1}{v} in (1)) [15], the crucial step is to conclude the relative compactness of the solution {vϵ}ϵ∈(0,1)\{v_{\epsilon}\}_{\epsilon\in(0,1)} to the corresponding regularization problem in Llockk−1​((0,∞),W1,kk−1​(Ω))L_{\rm loc}^{\frac{k}{k-1}}((0,\infty);W^{1,\frac{k}{k-1}}(\Omega)) with respect to the strong topology for k∈(2−1n,2)k\in(2-\frac{1}{n},2). Differently, for the system (1), we will firstly show that {vϵ}ϵ∈(0,1)\{v_{\epsilon}\}_{\epsilon\in(0,1)} has a uniform-in-time lower bound (indepedent of ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1)). Secondly, it will be derived that for some p>n​kn−1p>\frac{nk}{n-1} with k>2−1nk>2-\frac{1}{n} that {∇vϵvϵ}ϵ∈(0,1)\{\frac{\nabla v_{\epsilon}}{v_{\epsilon}}\Big\}_{\epsilon\in(0,1)} is relatively compact in Llocp​(Ω×(0,∞))L_{\rm loc}^{p}(\Omega\times(0,\infty)) with respect to the weak topology. Finally, upon selecting a suitable subsequence, we will obtain a global generalized solution for k>2−1nk>2-\frac{1}{n} with n≥2n\geq 2 by a standard compactness argument. Furthermore, if rμ\frac{r}{\mu} and the initial data u0u_{0} suitably small, this global generalized solution is in fact globally bounded.

Now, we state the main results of this paper.

Theorem 1

Let n≥2n\geq 2 and k>3​n−2nk>\frac{3n-2}{n}. If r,χ>0r,\chi>0 satisfying

r>{χ24,0<χ≤2,χ−1,χ>2,r>\begin{cases}\frac{\chi^{2}}{4},&0<\chi\leq 2,\\ \chi-1,&\chi>2,\end{cases} (1.25)

the problem (1) possesses a unique globally bounded classical solution.

Theorem 2

Let n≥2n\geq 2, k>2−1nk>2-\frac{1}{n} and r,χ>0r,\chi>0 satisfy (1.25). Then the system (1) admits at least a global generalized solution.

Theorem 3

Let (u,v)(u,v) be the global generalized solution for k∈(2−1n,3​n−2n]k\in(2-\frac{1}{n},\frac{3n-2}{n}] established in Theorem 2. Then for p>n⁡(n+2)2​(n+1)p>\frac{n(n+2)}{2(n+1)} there exist η,λ>0\eta,\lambda>0 small such that this solution is globally bounded provided rμ<η\frac{r}{\mu}<\eta and ∫Ωu0p​𝑑x<λ\int_{\Omega}u_{0}^{p}dx<\lambda.

Remark 1

Since 3​n−2n=2\frac{3n-2}{n}=2 for n=2n=2, we conclude by Theorem 1 with [20] that the classical solution to (1) for the case n=2n=2 must be globally bounded if k≥2k\geq 2. In addition, Theorems 2 and 3 show that k<2k<2 is permitted for the global existence-boundedness of solution to (1). This extends the global boundedness results for (1) with k=2k=2 obtained in [20].

Remark 2

Recall from [10, 30, 11] that the classical parabolic-elliptic chemotaxis system (1) possesses a global or further globally bounded classical (or generalized) solution if k>1k>1 and μ>0\mu>0 suitably large in logistic source r​u−μ​ukru-\mu u^{k}. While Theorems above say that the global solvability of solution to the system (1) requires not only the restriction on logistic kinetics but also the chemotactic sensitive coefficient χ>0\chi>0 properly small relative to r>0r>0, and the same were observed for the parabolic-parabolic case of system (1) [22]. Here the difficulty due to the singular sensitivity is substantial.

The rest part of the paper is arranged as follows. In Section 2, we will establish a uniform-in-time lower bound estimate on vv and demonstrate the global boundedness of the classical solution. Section 3 deals with the global existence of classical solution to the corresponding regularization problems. Then we prove the global existence and boundedness to the generalized solution to system (1) in Section 4.

2 Global boundedness of classical solutions

We at first give a lemma on the local existence of classical solutions to system (1) without proof, which can be obtained by the contraction argument as that in [20, Lemma 2.1].

{u∈C0​(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax)),v∈C2,0​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax)),\left\{\begin{aligned} &u\in C^{0}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T_{\max}))\cap C^{2,1}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,T_{\max})),\\[4.0pt] &v\in C^{2,0}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,T_{\max})),\end{aligned}\right.

for all ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1). Let k>2−2nk>2-\frac{2}{n}, μ>0\mu>0 and r,χ>0r,\chi>0 satisfy (2.5). Then the estimates in Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 are valid with Tmax,ϵ=∞T_{\max,\epsilon}=\infty and for all ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1). For convenience, we omits the new marks on these esitimates.

A similar arguments (the constants there are all independent of ϵ\epsilon) from (3.13) to (3.18), and in Lemma 2.4 with (3.8) indicate the estimate (3.11) for all ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1).  □\Box
